title: The Prideful 1
content:
It took all of a few days for Wei Wuxian to realize he’d made a massive mistake in life choices.

This damn donkey had the palate of a spoiled emperor. It refused to touch a single blade of grass unless it was fresh, tender, and dripping with morning dew; the second a tip turned even slightly yellow, the beast turned its nose up. Passing an old farmstead, Wei Wuxian swiped a handful of wheat straw to feed it. The creature gave it a couple of lazy chews, then spat it right back into his face—making a louder, ruder hacking noise than any human ever could. And if it wasn’t fed to its liking? It refused to budge. It threw full-blown temper tantrums, kicking its hind legs so violently that Wei Wuxian nearly caught hooves to the chin multiple times. To top it all off, its bray was like nails on a chalkboard.

Whether as a mount or a pampered pet, it was utterly, irredeemably useless.

Wei Wuxian couldn't help getting a little nostalgic for his sword. These days, it was probably hanging on the wall of some grand clan leader’s parlor, displayed as a trophy for company to gawk at.

After a grueling stretch of dragging, tugging, and practically pleading with the animal down the dirt roads, they hit a wide swathe of village farmland. The sun was baking the earth. Right along the ridge of the fields stood an enormous scholar tree, casting a wide umbrella of cool, dense shade over an old stone well. The locals had left a wooden bucket and a bamboo ladle perched on the rim for parched travelers. The spotted donkey trotted straight into the shadows and anchored its hooves to the dirt, stubbornly refusing to move another inch.

Wei Wuxian hopped down, giving its rump a wry pat. “Look at you, born with luxury tastes. You’re higher maintenance than I am.”

The donkey sneered and blew a wet snort into his face.

While he was idling in the shade, a small group materialized down the country paths.

They looked like salt-of-the-earth village folk, dressed in coarse homespun hemp and woven straw sandals, carrying handmade bamboo baskets on their backs. Walking among them was a girl with a round face—not a jaw-dropping beauty, but sweet and pleasantly demure. She looked wiped out from trudging under the blistering sun and clearly wanted to duck into the shade for a drink. But seeing a wild donkey stomping and braying by the tree, alongside a disheveled lunatic caked in chalky white powder and clownish red rouge, she froze in her tracks, too terrified to step closer.

Now, Wei Wuxian had always considered himself a consummate gentleman when it came to pretty girls. Taking the hint, he politely cleared out, shifting over to fuss with the donkey’s tether to give them space. Seeing he was harmless, the group finally let their guards down and shuffled into the shade. Drenched in sweat with cheeks flushed red from the heat, they collapsed under the tree, fanning their collars and hauling up bucketfuls of cool well water. The round-faced girl perched on the stone rim; realizing he’d moved out of courtesy, she gave Wei Wuxian a faint, grateful smile.

One of the men held a brass compass in his palms, squinting into the distance before staring down at the dial in deep confusion. “We’re practically at the base of Dafan Mountain. Why hasn't the needle twitched at all?”

The carvings and needles on this device were far too eerie for an ordinary compass. It didn't point north, south, east, or west—it tracked sinister entities and malevolent energy. It was a Compass of Evil.

Wei Wuxian immediately pegged them: an impoverished, rogue cultivator family from the sticks. Outside the aristocratic, diamond-crusted sects, the world was full of small households running modest family operations. They were probably trekking up from the countryside to crash with some distant, well-off relatives, or perhaps trying their luck on a night-hunt.

The middle-aged man leading them waved a ladle, calling everyone over to hydrate. “Maybe your compass is busted. I'll get you a new one later. Dafan Mountain is less than ten li out, so we can’t afford to lounge around. We've hauled ourselves all the way here—if we slack off now and let someone else beat us to the punch, this whole trip is a waste of shoe leather.”

A night-hunt it is.

The grand clans loved dressing things up in poetic airs, dubbing their monster-slaying travels "roving hunts." But because dark creatures generally prowled after sunset, people simply called them "night-hunts." The cultivation world was overflowing with minor clans, yet the names on everyone's lips were always the same few elites. Unless a family had generations of accumulated wealth and sacred treasures to fall back on, any small household dreaming of climbing the social ladder had to deliver cold, hard results. If you wanted respect and actual clout, you had to bag a vicious beast or put down a notorious monster.

Normally, this was right up Wei Wuxian's alley. But having hit the road only a few days ago, he’d raided a handful of random burial mounds only to dig up harmless, small-time spirits. What he really needed was a fearsome, heavy-hitting ghost general to act as his enforcer. Setting his sights forward, he decided he might as well try his luck on Dafan Mountain. If whatever was lurking up there proved useful, he’d tame it and recruit it for himself.

Having caught their breath, the travelers geared up to hit the road again. Before leaving, the round-faced girl fished an apple from her pack—small, half-green, half-red—and offered it out to him. “Here. For you.”

Wei Wuxian broke into a grin and reached out to take it, but the spotted donkey instantly craned its neck, teeth bared, snapping at the fruit. Wei Wuxian snatched his hand back just in time. Watching the donkey salivate over the little apple, inspiration struck. He grabbed a long branch, tied a strand of fishing line to the end, and dangled the apple right in front of the beast’s nose.

Smelling the sweet, crisp tang hovering inches from its jaws, the donkey lost its mind. Desperate to sink its teeth into the fruit that stayed forever just out of reach, it stretched its neck and sprinted forward like a rocket. The dust cloud it kicked up would put the most prized thoroughbreds to shame!

Riding the donkey’s manic charge, Wei Wuxian made it to the foot of Dafan Mountain before dusk had even fully fallen.

Only after arriving at the base did he realize what kind of "fan" the mountain was named for. Viewed from a distance, the peak bore an uncanny resemblance to a round, pot-bellied Buddha sitting comfortably against the sky—hence the name Dafan [Great Brahma]. Nestled right beneath the slope was a bustling hamlet aptly named Buddha's Foot Town.

The sheer volume of cultivators swarming the streets blew his expectations out of the water. It was an absolute free-for-all: disciples in a dizzying array of colorful clan robes and wandering rogues rubbed shoulders down every alley. Oddly enough, everyone looked wound tight as a bowstring. They were all so strung out that nobody even spared the mental bandwidth to laugh at the freak riding a donkey in corpse makeup.

Right in the middle of the main thoroughfare, a gaggle of cultivators had clustered together in heated debate. They’d started out quiet, but by the time Wei Wuxian trotted within earshot, the argument was boiling over:

“…I’m telling you, there’s no soul-consuming beast or soul-eating phantom around here! None of the compasses have picked up a single blip!”

“If there’s nothing out here, then how do you explain the seven townspeople who lost their souls?! Don’t tell me they all came down with the same mysterious flu! I sure as hell have never heard of a sickness that turns people into empty husks!”

“Just because the compass isn't spinning doesn't mean the beast doesn't exist! It only gives a rough bearing anyway—it’s hardly a precision instrument. For all we know, there’s something out there jamming the needle!”

“Do you even remember who invented the Compass of Evil? I’ve never heard of anything on earth being able to jam its reading!”

“What’s with the attitude? Why are you twisting my words? Of course I know Wei Ying built the damn thing! But it’s not like his work was flawless—are we not allowed to question it now?!”

“I never said you couldn't question it, and I certainly never claimed his craft was untouchable! Stop putting words in my mouth!”

Just like that, the argument careened completely off the rails into a personal grudge match. Wei Wuxian trotted past the squabbling mob on his donkey, chuckling quietly into his sleeve. All these years dead, and he was still the reigning champion of clan debates. Truly, whenever his name came up, blood pressures spiked. If the cultivation world held a vote for the most enduringly controversial figure in history, he’d sweep the ballot without even campaigning.

To be fair, the guy had a point. The Compass of Evil circulating today was just his rough first draft; it definitely lacked fine-tuned precision. He had actually been working on a refined prototype back then, but before he could roll it out, the sects had banded together to tear his house down. Everyone was simply stuck making do with the clunky beta version.

That said, creatures that gorged on raw flesh and chewed bone—like common walking corpses—were bottom-tier trash. Only higher-grade monsters or refined vengeful spirits had the palate and spiritual finesse to slurp down and digest human souls. And this thing had swallowed seven in one go! No wonder so many clans were swarming the mountain like flies. With a prize this dangerous on the loose, it wasn't surprising that a rudimentary compass was struggling to get a clean read.

Wei Wuxian tugged the makeshift rein, hopped off the donkey's back, and swung the bait down to its snout. “One bite. Just one… Hey! You’re trying to swallow my whole hand, you greedy beast!”

He wrenched the fruit back, took two bites out of the unchewed side, and shoved the core into the donkey’s grinding teeth. He paused for half a beat, deeply questioning the sequence of life choices that had brought him to splitting an apple with a farm animal, when someone bumped hard into his back.

He spun around to find a young girl. Even though she’d practically slammed into him, she didn't seem to notice he existed. Her eyes were completely hollow, a placid, vacant smile plastered across her face as she stared unblinkingly toward the distance.

Wei Wuxian traced her blank gaze. She was staring straight toward the dark, looming silhouette of the peak—Dafan Mountain.

Without a shred of warning, the girl began to dance right there in the dirt.

It was wild, chaotic thrashing, her limbs flailing like an animal trying to claw out of its skin. Wei Wuxian was watching the bizarre performance with genuine fascination when a middle-aged woman came sprinting down the lane, hiking up her skirts, throwing her arms around the girl in tears: “A-Yan! Come home with me, please, let's just go home!”

A-Yan shoved her off with shocking strength. That eerie, sweet smile never left her lips—dripping with a chilling, hollow benevolence—as she kept twirling and leaping down the street. The weeping mother had no choice but to chase after her through the market.

A roadside peddler clicked his tongue in pity. “What a sin… There goes the blacksmith’s girl, running wild again.”

“Her poor mother,” a bystander sighed. “First A-Yan, then her fiancé, and then her own husband… Not a single one spared.”

Wandering through the stalls and picking up scattered snippets of street gossip, Wei Wuxian managed to piece together the local disaster.

High on Dafan Mountain lay an ancient cemetery where generations of families from Buddha's Foot Town buried their dead, occasionally digging a fresh pit and planting a wooden marker for nameless drifters. A few months back, a massive storm had rolled in, tearing through the valley with howling winds and violent thunder. The relentless downpour triggered a devastating mudslide along the slopes—tearing right through the old graveyard. Scores of ancient plots were swept away. Several coffins were unearthed, their heavy lids blasted clean off by lightning strikes, charring the wood and the old bones inside to ash.

The townspeople had been deeply shaken. They staged grand prayer ceremonies and rebuilt the mounds, thinking the appease-the-spirits rituals had settled things. Instead, Buddha's Foot Town was hit with an epidemic of soulless husks.

The first victim was a notorious local deadbeat. Broke and allergic to hard work, he’d been up on the mountain chasing wild birds when the storm hit, getting trapped by the mudslide. He’d survived by the skin of his teeth, nearly scared to death. Bizarrely, a few days after limping home, he suddenly took a bride, throwing an extravagant wedding and swearing to turn over a new leaf to live an honest, upright life.

On his wedding night, he got blindingly drunk, collapsed into bed, and never got back up. When the new bride tried to wake him the next morning, he was entirely unresponsive. Shoving him, she realized his eyes were locked in a vacant stare and his skin was cold as ice. Aside from faint breathing, he was practically a corpse. He lay there like that for days without a drop of water or a grain of rice, until he quietly slipped into the dirt for good—leaving his bride a widow before the wedding wine had even gone stale.

The second victim was A-Yan, the blacksmith’s daughter. She’d just gotten engaged, only for her husband-to-be to get mauled to death by mountain wolves the very next day. When the news reached her, she collapsed with the exact same soulless stupor as the deadbeat. Mercifully, after some time, her spirit seemed to snap back into her body. But she’d lost her mind completely, spending every waking hour skipping through town with that unnerving smile, dancing for strangers.

The third victim was her father, Blacksmith Zheng.

Counting up to today, seven people had been hollowed out.

Wei Wuxian turned the clues over in his head. Ten to one, it’s a soul-eating phantom, not a beast.

The two classifications sounded similar, but they were entirely different breeds. Phantoms were born of resentful spirits, while beasts were demonic creatures of flesh and blood. Most likely, the mudslide had smashed open an old grave, lightning had shattered the seal, and whatever ancient evil had been slumbering beneath the soil was shaken awake. To know for sure, he just needed to take a look at the shattered coffin and see if any remnants of an old binding remained. But the villagers had undoubtedly reburied the bones and torched the wreckage months ago, leaving very little forensic evidence behind.

To reach the peak, one had to follow the mountain path leading out from the town. Wei Wuxian prodded the donkey along, meandering up the slope at a leisurely crawl. After winding up the trail for a stretch, he crossed paths with a group of cultivators heading down, their faces black with gloom.

A few of them were nursing fresh cuts, talking over each other in frustrated murmurs. In the dim dusk light, rounding a bend and slamming face-to-face with a lunatic in ghoul-white makeup riding a spotted donkey scared the living daylights out of them. They spat a few curses, swerved wide around him, and hurried down the trail.

Wei Wuxian glanced back, eyebrows raising. Did the monster prove too tough for them? Running home with their tails between their legs?

Shrugging it off, he tapped the donkey’s flank and broke into a steady trot, heading higher up the mountain.

He completely missed the furious complaints the retreating cultivators were venting into the night breeze:

“I’ve never met anyone so arrogant!”

“He’s the head of a premier Great Clan! What the hell is he doing down in the mud competing with us for a soul-eating phantom?! As if he didn't slay hundreds of those things back when he was young!”

“What can you do? He’s a Sect Leader. You can cross anyone in this world, but you never cross the Jiang Clan—and you never cross Jiang Cheng. Pack your things and let’s get out of here. Just chalk it up to rotten luck!”
